# Accumulating Validation

Validation that reports **every** failure at once, rather than throwing on the first one —
and that never constructs the object while it is still deciding whether the object should
exist.

Two properties, and the second is the one that gets missed.

## Why fail-fast is the wrong default at a boundary

Throwing on the first bad field is correct for an invariant violated inside a system. It is
wrong at an input boundary, where the caller is a person or another service:

- A form that reveals one error per submission takes five round trips to fill in five
  fields wrong, and each round trip is a chance to break a field that was previously fine.
- An API that returns one error per request cannot be driven by a client that wants to
  correct its payload, so the client guesses.
- A batch import that stops at the first bad row makes the operator discover the file's
  problems one deploy at a time.

The shape of the answer follows from the shape of the question: "is this valid?" has one
answer, but "what is wrong with this?" has a list.

## The part that is easy to miss

Exception-based validation usually runs *after* construction. The object is built, then
checked, then thrown away — which means a half-valid instance existed, was reachable, and
in a mutable design may have been stored, logged or passed to a listener before anyone
decided it was invalid.

Accumulating validation inverts that: gather the failures, and **construct only on the
empty-failure branch**. The type then carries a real guarantee — if you are holding one, it
passed. There is no state in which an invalid instance exists, so no code downstream needs
a defensive re-check, and no test needs to cover "what if a partially valid object gets
through".

```
validate(raw) -> Either[List[Error], TeamMember]
```

Errors are a list because there may be several; success is the constructed value because
there is nothing else to say.

## What it costs

The validators must be **independent**, since all of them run. Dependent checks — "this
field is required *when* that one is set" — either become one combined check or need
ordering, and pretending otherwise produces a cascade of confusing messages derived from a
single root cause. A missing file reported as five errors is worse than one.

The other cost is discipline about the error type. A list of strings is enough to display
and not enough to act on; a list of structured failures with a field reference is what lets
a client attach each message to its input. Compare the `details` object in
[[distributed-systems-protocol-labs]], which exists for the same reason.

## Relation to error-as-value

This is the boundary case of returning failures as values rather than raising them. The
same rebuild applies it throughout: `Either` and validated result types instead of `null`,
unchecked casts, or sentinel numbers — each of which is a failure the type system was
offering to catch for free. See [[functional-programming-scala-laboratories]].
